rows.notes: The paper is explicitly a literature review (Sustainability, article type 'Review'). Its only own analysis is a descriptive satellite-derived soil moisture and GRACE groundwater percentile timeline for the three HPA regions (Section 3.2, Figure 7), which does not concern SDI. All statements on sub-surface drip irrigation (Section 4.3: up to 45% water reduction, 97% application efficiency, Nebraska and Texas corn results, cotton in North Texas) are drawn from cited works [67-73], not from the authors' own experiments. The recommendation that SDI could extend aquifer life in vulnerable regions is a synthesis/opinion, not a measured result on aquifer lifespan or recharge.

Same review paper. Section 4.2 on soil moisture sensing compiles cited evidence (Kansas groundwater management districts [61], Texas OAP cost-saving projection [62], Colorado recommendations [63], Nebraska Corn Board [64]) and USDA survey statistics on scheduling methods [9]; none is the authors' own result. The authors' own remote-sensing soil moisture analysis (Section 3.2) characterises regional drought, not the effect of sensors on water use or aquifer lifespan. The claim that sensor-based scheduling could reduce extractions and extend aquifer life is argued, not demonstrated.

notes: Full text appears complete (pages 1-17 with references). The paper is a narrative review with a small descriptive GIS/remote-sensing component on soil moisture and groundwater storage percentiles that does not test any irrigation technology; hence Q1 is answered 'no' for both claim rows as the review supplies no primary evidence on the cited claims.
